H1.text: A swing drops, and your stomach floats. A diver feels weightless in the air. Astronauts float in their station.

H3.text: Diya takes the hospital lift up to visit a patient. As it starts, she feels heavier.

H4.text: As it stops at the top floor, she feels lighter. Did her weight change, or something else?

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will know exactly what she feels, with one short formula.

P2.text: Your true weight is m g, the Earth's pull. In the lift, it does not change.

P3.text: But you never feel gravity directly. You feel the floor pushing up on your feet.

P4.text: In episode sixty, we saw that a scale reads that push, the normal force N.

P5.text: So your apparent weight is N. And N can change, even when m g does not.

S1.text: Let's run it. Diya, fifty kilograms, stands on a scale in the lift.

S2.text: At rest, the scale reads fifty kilograms. N equals m g.

S3.text: The lift starts up, speeding up at one metre per second squared.

S4.text: The scale jumps to fifty five point one. The floor must push harder, to speed her up.

S5.text: Now it rises at a steady two metres per second. a is zero, so the reading is back to fifty.

S6.text: Near the top floor, it slows down. Now a points down.

S7.text: The scale drops to forty four point nine. She feels lighter, though she is still going up.

S9.text: The velocity points up. The acceleration points down. The scale follows the acceleration, not the velocity.

D1.text: Now the formula, step by step. Take up as positive.

D2.text: Step one. Two forces act on Diya. N from the scale, up. And her weight, m g, down.

D3.text: Step two. Newton's second law. N minus m g equals m a.

D4.text: Step three. So N equals m times g plus a. Speeding up going up, a is up, and N is more than m g.

D5.text: Step four. If a points down, N equals m times g minus a. She feels lighter.

D6.text: Step five. In free fall, a equals g. N is m times g minus g. Zero.

T1.text: Remember this. A scale reads N, and N follows the acceleration, not the velocity.

C2.text: Going up, but slowing down. The acceleration points down, so N is less than m g.

C3.text: Going down, and speeding up. The acceleration points down again. Lighter again.

C4.text: Now you try. The lift goes down, and slows to stop at the ground floor. Does Diya feel heavier or lighter? Pause and decide.

C5.text: Heavier! Slowing a downward motion needs an upward acceleration, so N is more than m g.

R1.text: So what is weightlessness? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. A box falls freely, with a scale and an apple inside.

R3.text: Two. Box, scale and apple all fall with acceleration g.

R4.text: Three. So the scale has nothing to push on. N is zero, and the reading is zero.

R5.text: Four. The apple still has its weight. It just feels nothing holding it up. That is weightlessness.

K1.text: One more. In a space station, does gravity still pull on the astronauts? Pause and think.

K2.text: Yes! Up there, gravity is almost nine tenths as strong. They float because they and the station fall together, round the Earth.

W2.text: A sixty kilogram man is in the lift. It speeds up going down, at one point eight metres per second squared. What does the scale read?

W3.text: The acceleration points down, so N equals m times g minus a.

W4.text: N is sixty, times nine point eight minus one point eight. Sixty times eight. Four hundred and eighty newtons.

W5.text: The scale shows N over g. Four eighty over nine point eight. About forty nine kilograms.

W6.text: If the lift fell freely, a would be g, and the scale would read zero.

X2.text: Many students think going up means heavier, and going down means lighter.

X3.text: But only the acceleration counts. Going up while slowing down, you feel lighter.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In lift numericals, often with a velocity time graph.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A sixty kilogram man stands on a scale in a lift. From rest, it speeds up to three metres per second in two seconds going up, moves steadily, then stops in three seconds. g is ten. Find the ratio of the largest to the smallest reading while it moves. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Twenty three to eighteen.

A2.text: Speeding up, a is plus one point five. N is sixty times eleven point five. Six hundred and ninety.

A3.text: Stopping, a is minus one. N is sixty times nine. Five hundred and forty.

A4.text: Six ninety over five forty is twenty three over eighteen.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. What does a scale actually measure?

Y3.text: Two. The lift goes up and slows down. Do you feel heavier or lighter, and why?

Y4.text: Three. Why do astronauts float, even though gravity still pulls on them?

N1.text: Next time, a new chapter. Push a wall all day, and it never moves. Did you do any work? We find out in work, energy and power.
